newsitem.title: ISRAEL: After summit, intifada atmosphere pervades Gaza.
newsitem.headline: After summit, intifada atmosphere pervades Gaza.

text.p: The sounds of revolt echoed through the tense streets of Gaza on Thursday, reviving the spirit of a Palestinian uprising that the Middle East peace process was supposed to have ended.
A day after an emergency Israeli-Arab summit in Washington ending in what Palestinians considered failure, nationalist songs blared from shops, cars and homes.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, trying to douse Arab fury that erupted last week when he opened a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem, returned to Israel saying life was now safer for Israeli children.

But in the Gaza Strip, Palestinian schoolchildren prepared for a possible new wave of violence if peace talks due to resume on Sunday fail, scouring the streets for stones and gathering tyres to burn as roadblocks.
"Let's look for tyres and hide them just in case something happens," said one schoolchild.
Israel kept tanks poised on the edges of Palestinian towns in a show of force.
Palestinian street artists did some sabre-rattling of their own.

Slogans of the intifada, the 1987 to 1993 Palestinian uprising against Israeli occupation, reappeared on walls cleaned of graffiti after Yasser Arafat returned to Gaza in 1994 under the now-threatened peace deal with Israel.
Walls were also plastered with posters of young Palestinian men killed in last week's clashes which claimed 58 Arab and 15 Jewish lives.

A giant mural of a bare-chested, muscular Palestinian president bursting through a Jewish Star of David -- Jerusalem's al-Aqsa mosque in his hands -- adorned a stadium in the southern Gazan town of Khan Younis during a rally of Arafat's Fatah faction.
Music stores did a brisk business.

"The people's demand for national songs has increased a lot. They are also buying songs of the intifada and this shows you how they really feel deep within," said Osama Kalloub, an employee at a Gaza City music shop.
Palestinian officials called the Washington summit a failure, noting Netanyahu had refused any timetable for a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank city of Hebron.
Palestinians, worried by Israeli tanks outside their towns, prepared for the worst despite agreement by Israel and the PLO to start continuous negotiations on Sunday.
In some West Bank cities popular committees, dormant since the intifada, have been reactivated.

"These unarmed committees are coordinating with Palestinian security forces. Their duties will be to advise people and help the wounded in case confrontations take place," said Qaddoura Moussa, a Fatah activist.
Palestinians also have begun to stockpile food and supplies.
"People are frantically stocking up, mainly on flour. This is similar to the days of intifada," said Nablus shopkeeper Kamal Kalboneh.
